title: 178 Cannabinoid transference and retention in tissues of beef steers fed hemp leaves
content:
Abstract
Hemp, Cannabis sativa L., is a versatile and environmentally sustainable crop that has recently been approved for production in the U.S. under certain regulations. Hemp production is accompanied by by-products that, if not utilized in human markets, are wasted. Previous research indicates that hemp leaves are nutritionally viable for use as livestock feed, particularly for ruminants. However, the presence of cannabinoids restricts hemp inclusion in livestock diets in the U.S. as these compounds can be retained in edible tissues and transferred to humans. The objective of this study was to analyze the uptake and depletion profiles of circulating cannabinoids in rumen fluid, blood plasma, adipose tissue, and feces of beef steers fed hemp leaves. The trial included two × 14-d periods followed by a 45-d monitoring period. In period 1 (CON), five ruminally cannulated steers were fed hay (8.0% crude protein). In period 2 (EXP), steers consumed hay and were supplemented with hemp leaves at 3.9 mg/kg BW cannabidiolic acid (CBDA) mixed with alfalfa cubes at 0.2% BW. During the monitoring period, steers grazed grass pasture with ad libitum access to water without hemp supplementation. Accumulation of the four most abundant cannabinoids in the hemp (i.e., CBDA, cannabidiol [CBD], tetrahydrocannabidiolic acid [THCA-A] and delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol [D9-THC]) were measured in cattle tissues at various timepoints. Dietary hemp exposure resulted in accumulation of cannabinoids, including THC derivatives, in all tissues analyzed with persistence observed over time (i.e., up to 96 h in blood and up to 6 weeks in adipose tissue). CBDA and CBD were present in detectable levels in all tissues sampled. D9-THC was not detected in blood plasma but was present in detectable amounts in the rumen fluid (2.0 ± 0.6 ng/mL), adipose tissue (8.4 ± 5.0 ng/mL), and feces (253 ± 228 ng/g). THCA-A was present in detectable amounts in all samples except for adipose tissue. There were differences in the accumulation of acidic cannabinoids (CBDA and THCA-A) versus decarboxylated (CBD and D9-THC) across tissues such that acidic cannabinoids were more prevalent in rumen fluid, blood plasma, and feces whereas the decarboxylated cannabinoids were more concentrated in adipose tissue. In rumen fluid sampled during hemp supplementation, CBDA:CBD was 4.55:1. In blood plasma and feces sampled after hemp supplementation ceased, CBDA:CBD was 56.7:1 and 3.32:1, respectively. However, in adipose tissue sampled after hemp feeding ceased, CBDA:CBD was 0.14:1. This suggests that cannabinoids undergo some form of biotransformation in the body which could be driven by the rumen, however, further research is needed.
